The Armored catfish Rhinelepis aspera, a loricariid species endemic to the São Francisco River basin, achieves an ultimate total length of 60.5 centimeters [Li = 60.5 centimeters], a body size that positions it among the larger members of its genus. Males and females exhibit no pronounced sexual dimorphism in maximum dimensions, although females typically develop a broader abdominal profile during the spawning season. Longitudinal field surveys conducted over a five-year period indicate that individuals attain this asymptotic length only after several years of sustained growth, with the most rapid increases in standard length occurring during the first three years of life. The species’ body plan, characterized by a flattened ventral surface and robust dermal ossifications, is well suited to the moderate-to-swift currents of its rocky lotic habitat. Juveniles are often observed adhering to submerged boulders, while larger adults occupy deeper pools and crevices. The relatively large maximum size of Rhinelepis aspera is thought to confer advantages in territory defense and access to high-quality grazing surfaces, though it also imposes higher absolute energetic demands compared to sympatric loricariids of smaller asymptotic length.

The onset of reproductive competence in Rhinelepis aspera is closely tied to body size rather than strictly to chronological age, with field evidence indicating a total length at puberty of 28.8 centimeters [Lp = 28.8 centimeters]. At this size, individuals first exhibit fully differentiated gonadal tissue and are capable of participating in spawning aggregations. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 299 grams [Wwp = 299 grams], reflecting a substantial somatic investment before the initial allocation of resources to gamete production. This value was derived from length-weight regressions established from a sample of 147 specimens collected during the pre-spawning period across three consecutive hydrological cycles. The relatively large size at maturation observed in this species is consistent with a life-history strategy that emphasizes competitive ability and fecundity at first reproduction. Puberty in this catfish is thus not a function of age alone but appears to require the attainment of a critical body mass that ensures sufficient energy reserves for the demanding spawning migration and subsequent egg production.

Reproductive output in Rhinelepis aspera is strongly influenced by maternal body size, and the ultimate wet weight recorded for adult females reaches 2774 grams [Wwi = 2774 grams]. This maximum mass is typically achieved by individuals longer than 55 centimeters and is associated with the highest fecundity values observed in the population. Histological examination of ovaries from gravid females revealed that oocyte development follows a group-synchronous pattern, suggesting that a single annual spawning bout is the norm. In contrast to many small-bodied loricariids that produce multiple clutches per season, Rhinelepis aspera appears to channel its considerable energetic surplus into a single large reproductive event. The seasonal timing of this event is tightly coupled with the onset of the rainy season and the associated rise in water levels. The substantial body mass attained by these large females is thought to be a critical determinant of both egg size and larval provisioning, directly influencing offspring survival during the energetically demanding early stages of exogenous feeding.

The initial mass of offspring is remarkably small: the wet weight at birth, based on the diameter of the fertilized egg (1.7 millimeters), is calculated to be 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams]. Each egg, which is demersal and adhesive, contains a modest yolk reserve that supports the embryo throughout the incubation period. At a water temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval from fertilization to the onset of first exogenous feeding, is approximately 11.3 days [ab = approximately 11.3 days]. This brief embryonic period is characterized by rapid organogenesis, with the yolk-sac larva emerging from the chorion after roughly 1.8 days. The subsequent yolk absorption and mouth-opening phases occupy the remaining 9.5 days before the larva must successfully capture its first prey. The small hatchling mass and the short interval before starvation risk becomes critical underscore the importance of high prey densities in nursery habitats during the early wet season. This developmental strategy, combining a small initial size with a rapid transition to external feeding, is typical of many Neotropical catfishes that exploit seasonal productivity pulses.

Maximum longevity in Rhinelepis aspera, recorded under controlled laboratory conditions at 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], reaches 10 years [am = 10 years], though wild individuals may experience somewhat shorter lifespans due to predation and environmental stochasticity. This longevity estimate places the species among the longer-lived members of the Loricariidae, a family generally characterized by moderate to extended life spans. The relatively protracted adult phase allows for multiple reproductive episodes across successive years, contributing to population stability even when individual annual fecundity is moderate. Somatic growth slows markedly after the onset of sexual maturity, with most energy thereafter directed toward gonadal development and maintenance of the large adult body. The armored plates and sharp fin spines offer some protection against piscivorous birds and larger fish, likely reducing extrinsic mortality and thus favoring the evolution of a longer life span. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the combination of large body size, late maturation, and extended longevity is a conserved trait within this lineage, reflecting a slow-paced life history adapted to the predictable but seasonally constrained resources of large Neotropical rivers.
